title: A piece above your level
summary: With your teacher, choose one harder piece and plan learning it across the whole sprint, not one week.
materials: the piece from your teacher, with a pencil

figure.alt: Three boxes stacked, one for each of the next three weeks of this sprint. The piece above your level is planned across all three, not learned in this one week alone.

steps.title: A piece above your level
steps.body:
Every trick from four seasons was built for a piece exactly at your level. This one is not at your level. It is a stretch, chosen with your teacher on purpose, and it will not be finished this week or even this sprint's first half.

1. With your teacher, choose one piece harder than your usual pieces.
2. Break it into small sections, smaller than usual, spread across the next three weeks, not just this one.
3. Learn only the first section this week, hard bars first, more slowly than feels comfortable.
4. Write a plan for the next three weeks: which section, in which week, so the sprint does not run out before the piece does.

A piece above your level is not meant to feel easy by week four. It is meant to still be a little hard, and a little further along than it was.

figure.alt: A one-octave keyboard from middle C, with the A above middle C highlighted, the note sung or played loudly with the sustain pedal held silently down, to hear whether that string answers back on its own.

steps.title: Resonance: things sing along
steps.body:
A string can start vibrating on its own when the right note reaches it through the air, without anyone striking it. That is resonance. The sustain pedal lifts every damper at once, so every string is free to answer a matching pitch if one arrives.

Predict first: press the sustain pedal down silently, with no key struck. Guess whether singing the A above middle C, which wiggles 440 times a second, will make that same string hum back on its own. Write your guess in the Practice log.

Measure: press the pedal down silently, then sing or play that A loudly close to the strings. Let go of the pedal and listen carefully to what you hear stop.

Compare: did a string answer back, and did it stop when the dampers came down?

Teach it: explain why an open piano can seem to hum after a loud sound in the room, with no key pressed at all.

figure.alt: Two boxes stacked: section one, shaded, learned by the third sitting this week, and section two, unshaded, only just begun.

steps.title: Four sittings
steps.body: Fifteen minutes each. Tick a sitting when it is done. Days do not matter; sittings do.
checklist: Sitting 1: with the teacher's plan, learn the first two bars of section one
Sitting 2: the rest of section one, hard bars first, slowly
Sitting 3: section one clean, start on the first bars of section two
Sitting 4: everything learned so far, once through, then once as if recording
An old piece played once, at your usual level, for balance

steps.title: Record this week's version
steps.prompt: Play everything you have learned of the harder piece so far, once through, hands in the frame.
